\section{Supervised and Model-Internal Signal Analysis}\label{app:supervised_combination}

\subsection{Supervised Signal Combination}

Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
Neither handcrafted signal combinations nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.

\subsection{Hidden State Probes}\label{app:hidden_probe}

The preceding negative results suggest the bottleneck is model-internal rather than a feature engineering problem.
We test this directly by training probes on the generating model's hidden representations.

\paragraph{Setup.}
For each of $N{=}8$ samples per instance, we extract the mean-pooled final-layer hidden state ($d{=}4096$) from the generating Qwen3-8B model and train a linear probe and a two-layer MLP (hidden dim${=}256$) to predict per-sample F1 (5-fold CV, 3 seeds).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Hidden state probes vs.\ LP for sample selection (5-fold CV ${\times}$ 3 seeds). $\rho$: Spearman correlation with per-sample F1. Sel.\ F1: selection F1. Gap\%: oracle gap closure. SciERC greedy${=}0.644$, oracle${=}0.775$.}
\label{tab:hidden_probe}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l ccc cc@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Few-NERD}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6}
Method & $\rho$ & Sel.\ F1 & Gap\% & $\rho$ & Gap\% \\
\midrule
LP & .283 & $\mathbf{.650}$ & $+$4.8 & .606 & 12.3 \\
Hidden Linear & $.179{\pm}.019$ & $.613{\pm}.002$ & $-$23.4 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{---} \\
Hidden MLP & $\mathbf{.388{\pm}.013}$ & $.637{\pm}.003$ & $-$5.1 & $\mathbf{.629{\pm}.007}$ & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Cross-dataset asymmetry.}
On SciERC, the MLP probe achieves higher quality correlation than LP ($\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ $0.283$, $+37$\%); hidden states encode information beyond what LP captures.
Yet higher correlation does not yield better selection: MLP selection F1 ($0.637$) falls below LP's ($0.650$), with gap closure turning negative ($-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Table~\ref{tab:hidden_probe}).
The linear probe performs worse still ($\rho{=}0.179$, gap closure $-23.4$\%).
On Few-NERD, the MLP provides no increment over LP (gap closure $11.7$\% vs.\ $12.3$\%).
A learned token-level LP aggregator (1D CNN over per-token log-probabilities) matches mean LP on Few-NERD (gap closure $56.4$\% vs.\ $55.8$\%); LP's bottleneck is not token aggregation.
The correlation-selection gap extends to model-internal representations: in the high-capability regime (greedy F1${=}0.644$), inter-sample F1 differences are small enough that improved ranking provides no marginal selection value, consistent with the capability-diversity tension (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Multi-Seed Stability}\label{app:multiseed}

Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} reports quality estimation metrics across three random seeds for both model families on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
On NER, the signal ranking VC${>}$SJ${>}$EM${>}$FK${>}$LP is identical across all six model-seed combinations, with $\sigma{\leq}0.025$ for all signals (rankings are stable across our 3 seeds, though statistical power with $n{=}3$ is limited).
On RE (Qwen only, preliminary), VC remains the top signal ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM. This reversal from the NER ranking reflects RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
LLaMA absolute values are systematically lower than Qwen on NER, consistent with the directionally-consistent-but-magnitude-dependent characterization in the main text.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Multi-seed quality estimation on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seeds: 42, 123, 456). NER: both models; RE: Qwen only (preliminary). Signal ranking is stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.025$). $\sigma$ is population standard deviation over 3 seeds.}
\label{tab:multiseed}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
& LP & FK & SJ & VC & EM \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{NER Spearman $\rho$ (mean $\pm\sigma$)}} \\
Qwen & .217${\pm}$.013 & .254${\pm}$.016 & .364${\pm}$.018 & .386${\pm}$.019 & .307${\pm}$.008 \\
LLaMA & .162${\pm}$.025 & .256${\pm}$.024 & .325${\pm}$.021 & .384${\pm}$.014 & .279${\pm}$.011 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{RE Spearman $\rho$ (mean $\pm\sigma$, Qwen)}} \\
Qwen & .297${\pm}$.022 & .290${\pm}$.012 & .249${\pm}$.002 & .309${\pm}$.024 & .135${\pm}$.016 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{NER AUROC (mean $\pm\sigma$)}} \\
Qwen & .579${\pm}$.008 & .600${\pm}$.016 & .659${\pm}$.016 & .677${\pm}$.011 & .631${\pm}$.013 \\
LLaMA & .565${\pm}$.008 & .593${\pm}$.006 & .632${\pm}$.012 & .673${\pm}$.009 & .606${\pm}$.005 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

\section{Training Configuration}\label{app:training}
